title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
hookLine: a father cries I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief

lines: A FATHER TOO TIRED TO BE POLITE.
cards: A hospital hallway, someone you love behind the door, and no news: that's where this father has been living. Jesus comes down the mountain into an argument: a crowd, some scribes, and the other disciples, who've failed.
A man brought his son to them. Since childhood the boy has had fits: a spirit throws him down, he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, goes rigid. It has thrown him into fire and into water.
The disciples couldn't help. Now the father turns to Jesus, too tired to be polite.

teach.b: First, the request: if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us. If you can. Some readers hear years of disappointment in those three words.

teach.h: ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO HIM THAT BELIEVETH.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." The question isn't whether Jesus can. It's whether the father can believe.
Third, the cry. Mark says the father cried out at once, with tears: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." I believe.
I don't believe enough. Both true at once. And Jesus doesn't wait for a purer faith.

teach.h: HE HEALS WITH THE FAITH THERE IS.
teach.b: He heals the boy with the faith this man actually has, half of it doubt. The boy goes still as a corpse, and people say he's dead. Jesus takes him by the hand and lifts him, and he stands up.
Fourth, afterward, indoors, the disciples ask why they couldn't do it.
In the Douay: "This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting."

teach.h: I DO BELIEVE, LORD: HELP MY UNBELIEF.
teach.b: The failure, as Jesus names it, wasn't technique. This needed prayer. And the father's cry has stayed in Catholic prayer: short enough to say in a hallway, honest enough for the nights when faith is thin.

how: Catholics use the father's words from Mark 9 as a short prayer in times of doubt, and the Catechism describes faith as seeking understanding.

o: a settled conviction that God does not exist
faith that wavers, or falls short of trust
suspicion that someone is lying to you

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: all things are possible to him that believeth

s: Jesus waits until the father's faith is perfect
he heals the boy with the faith the father actually has, doubt and all.
the other disciples tried first and failed
the father brought his son to them, and they could not cast the spirit out.
the boy's trouble had started only recently
his father says it has been so from his infancy.

games.q: you're the father. Jesus says all things are possible to the one who believes. you believe, and you also don't. what do you say?
o: say you're not sure and walk away.
cry out that you believe, and ask for help with your unbelief.
games.why: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." he brings both halves, and Jesus heals his son.

practice: Notice how much you believe today, about God, about yourself, about anything that matters to you, without inflating it or shrinking it.

If you pray, say the father's words slowly on your breath: I do believe, Lord, breathing in; help my unbelief, breathing out. If you don't, simply let both be true at once, the part of you that trusts and the part that doesn't.

wordCard.voice: Unbelief. What a desperate father confessed to Jesus in the same breath as his faith: I do believe, Lord, help my unbelief. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: help my unbelief. apistia is faith with a 'not' in front of it.

carryVoice: Your line: bring your doubt along. The father brought his, and Jesus didn't send him away. See you tomorrow.
